summary: vvaharness scanned acme-payments-api (Python/FastAPI) end to end. Twelve findings were confirmed across all five severities, including a critical SQL injection in the payment query builder and hardcoded AWS credentials in the settings module. Two exploit chains link the credential and injection findings to broader compromise. One low-confidence finding (a TODO comment) was verified as a false positive: the referenced route is dead code behind a disabled debug flag.

finding.title: SQL injection in payment query builder
finding.verdict_reason: Confirmed by tracing the merchant_ref query parameter into a raw SQL string.
finding.description: User-supplied merchant_ref is string-formatted directly into a raw SQL query used to look up payment records.
finding.impact: Full compromise of the payments table (read/write), including card-reference tokens and settlement amounts.
finding.exploit_scenario: An authenticated merchant sends a crafted merchant_ref (e.g. `' OR '1'='1`) to /api/payments/search, which is interpolated into the WHERE clause and returns other merchants' transactions.
preconditions: Caller must be able to reach /api/payments/search (any authenticated merchant).
finding.recommendation: Use a parameterized query (SQLAlchemy bound parameters) instead of an f-string; add a regression test asserting the query is never built via string formatting.
finding.code_snippet: query = f"SELECT * FROM payments WHERE merchant_ref = '{merchant_ref}'"
finding.verifier_reasoning: Traced merchant_ref from the FastAPI path operation through to the raw cursor.execute() call with no sanitization in between.
finding.offensive_reason: Directly reachable by any authenticated user with no additional preconditions.
finding.exploitability_notes: No input validation or allowlisting precedes the query; the exploit path requires only a valid session, not elevated privileges.

findings.exploitability_notes: No input validation or allowlisting precedes the query; the exploit path requires only a valid session, not elevated privileges.

finding.title: Hardcoded AWS credentials in settings module
finding.verdict_reason: Key pattern and format match a live AWS access key ID.
finding.description: A hardcoded AWS access key/secret pair is committed to the settings module and shipped in every build artifact.
finding.impact: Anyone with repo or artifact access can assume the AWS credentials and access the S3 buckets and SES sending identity they authorize.
finding.exploit_scenario: An attacker who obtains the built container image (e.g. from a leaked internal registry) extracts the key from settings.py and uses it directly against the AWS API.
preconditions: Attacker has read access to the source tree, a build artifact, or a leaked container image.
finding.recommendation: Rotate the exposed key immediately, remove it from source control history, and load credentials from the environment or a secrets manager instead.
finding.verifier_reasoning: Confirmed the string matches the AKIA prefix format and is read directly by boto3.client() elsewhere in the module.
finding.offensive_reason: Any party with source or artifact access gets standing AWS credentials.
finding.exploitability_notes: Static string in a tracked file — no runtime interaction needed to extract it.

findings.exploitability_notes: Static string in a tracked file — no runtime interaction needed to extract it.

finding.title: SSRF in webhook URL fetcher
finding.verdict_reason: The fetcher follows redirects and has no destination allowlist.
finding.description: The outbound-webhook test endpoint fetches an arbitrary merchant-supplied URL server-side with no destination allowlist.
finding.impact: Can be used to reach internal-only services (metadata endpoints, admin consoles) from the application's network position.
finding.exploit_scenario: A merchant configures a webhook URL pointing at the cloud metadata endpoint (169.254.169.254) via the 'test webhook' feature and reads the response back through the test-result API.
preconditions: Merchant-role account needed to reach the webhook test feature.
finding.recommendation: Resolve and validate the target host against an allowlist (or block RFC1918/link-local ranges) before issuing the outbound request.
finding.verifier_reasoning: Verified webhook_url is user-supplied and unfiltered before reaching requests.get().
finding.offensive_reason: Requires only a merchant account, no elevated role.
finding.exploitability_notes: No egress filtering observed in the deployment manifests reviewed.

findings.exploitability_notes: No egress filtering observed in the deployment manifests reviewed.

finding.title: JWT signature verification can be bypassed
finding.verdict_reason: The alg parameter is read from the token header, enabling alg=none.
finding.description: jwt.decode() is called with algorithms taken from the token's own header rather than a fixed server-side allowlist, permitting an alg=none token.
finding.impact: An attacker can forge a valid-looking session for any user ID.
finding.exploit_scenario: An attacker crafts a JWT with header {"alg": "none"} and an arbitrary payload, sends it as the bearer token, and is treated as authenticated.
finding.recommendation: Pin the accepted algorithm list to the one the server issues tokens with (e.g. algorithms=["HS256"]) and reject alg=none explicitly.
finding.verifier_reasoning: Confirmed algorithms= is derived from attacker-controlled input, not a server-side constant.
finding.exploitability_notes: No additional network position or credentials required.

findings.exploitability_notes: No additional network position or credentials required.

finding.title: Path traversal in invoice download endpoint
finding.verdict_reason: The filename query parameter reaches open() with only a naive '..' strip.
finding.description: The invoice-download endpoint builds a filesystem path from a user-supplied filename with only a naive '..' string replace, which does not stop encoded or nested traversal sequences.
finding.impact: Read access to arbitrary files on the API host readable by the service account.
finding.exploit_scenario: An authenticated user requests /api/invoices/download?filename=..%2f..%2f..%2fetc%2fpasswd and receives the file's contents.
finding.recommendation: Resolve the path with os.path.realpath and verify it stays under the invoices directory before opening; reject requests that fail the check.
finding.verifier_reasoning: Traced filename from the query string to open() with no realpath/prefix check in between.
finding.exploitability_notes: URL-encoding and repeated separators bypass the single-pass replace.

findings.exploitability_notes: URL-encoding and repeated separators bypass the single-pass replace.

finding.title: No rate limiting on OTP verification endpoint
finding.verdict_reason: No throttle or lockout observed on the verify path.
finding.description: The OTP verification endpoint has no per-account or per-IP rate limit, allowing an unbounded number of guesses against a 6-digit code.
finding.impact: Increases the practical odds of a successful OTP brute-force within the code's validity window.
finding.exploit_scenario: An attacker scripts repeated POSTs to /api/auth/otp/verify for a known email, cycling all 10^6 codes before expiry.
preconditions: Knowledge of a target email address.
finding.recommendation: Add a per-account attempt counter with exponential backoff and a hard cap before requiring a fresh OTP request.
finding.code_snippet: def verify_otp(email: str, code: str): ...  # no attempt tracking
finding.verifier_reasoning: Confirmed no rate-limit decorator or attempt-count check on this route, unlike /api/auth/login which has one.
finding.offensive_reason: Pre-auth, but requires sustained request volume.
finding.exploitability_notes: 6-digit numeric space is brute-forceable within typical OTP TTLs absent throttling.

findings.exploitability_notes: 6-digit numeric space is brute-forceable within typical OTP TTLs absent throttling.

finding.title: Stack traces returned in API error responses
finding.verdict_reason: The debug exception handler is registered unconditionally.
finding.description: The global exception handler returns the full traceback and local variable dump in the JSON response body for any unhandled exception.
finding.impact: Discloses internal file paths, library versions, and occasionally query parameters or partial secrets held in local variables.
finding.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends a request that triggers an unhandled exception (e.g. a malformed multipart body) and reads the stack trace from the response.
finding.recommendation: Register the debug traceback handler only when DEBUG=true, and return a generic 500 body with a correlation ID in production.
finding.verifier_reasoning: Confirmed debug_traceback_handler is unconditional, not gated on an env flag.
finding.offensive_reason: Aids further exploitation but isn't independently exploitable.
finding.exploitability_notes: No authentication required to trigger a 500 and read the traceback.

findings.exploitability_notes: No authentication required to trigger a 500 and read the traceback.

finding.title: CORS allows any origin with credentials
finding.description: CORSMiddleware is configured with a wildcard origin alongside allow_credentials=True, which most browsers will reflect as an always-allowed origin, exposing cookie-authenticated endpoints to any site.
finding.impact: A malicious site visited by a logged-in user can read authenticated API responses cross-origin.
finding.exploit_scenario: A victim with an active session visits an attacker page that issues a fetch() with credentials: 'include' against the API and reads the JSON response.
preconditions: Victim has an active authenticated session in the same browser.
finding.recommendation: Replace the wildcard with an explicit allowlist of trusted frontend origins.
finding.verifier_reasoning: Confirmed both allow_origins="*" and allow_credentials=True are set together, which is the specific insecure combination.
finding.offensive_reason: Needs a logged-in victim to visit a malicious page.
finding.exploitability_notes: Requires a victim to visit an attacker-controlled page while logged in.

findings.exploitability_notes: Requires a victim to visit an attacker-controlled page while logged in.

finding.title: Password hashing uses a low bcrypt cost factor
finding.verdict_reason: bcrypt.gensalt(rounds=4) is well below the recommended cost factor.
finding.description: Passwords are hashed with bcrypt at a cost factor of 4, far below the current recommendation of 12+, making offline brute-force cheaper.
finding.impact: Reduces the cost of cracking a stolen password hash table.
finding.exploit_scenario: Given a leaked hash table (e.g. via the SQL injection finding above), an attacker cracks weakly-hashed passwords far faster than at a proper cost factor.
preconditions: Attacker already has the password hash (chained from another finding).
finding.recommendation: Raise the bcrypt cost factor to at least 12 and rehash on next login.
finding.verifier_reasoning: Confirmed the rounds= literal is 4 versus the library default of 12.
finding.offensive_reason: Only relevant after another finding exposes the hash table.
finding.exploitability_notes: Only matters if hashes are already exfiltrated; not independently reachable.

findings.exploitability_notes: Only matters if hashes are already exfiltrated; not independently reachable.

finding.title: Missing HSTS header on API responses
finding.verdict_reason: No Strict-Transport-Security header is set on any response.
finding.description: The API never sends a Strict-Transport-Security header, so a client's first plaintext request is not upgraded to HTTPS automatically.
finding.impact: Slightly increases exposure to protocol-downgrade / SSL-stripping attacks on the first connection.
finding.exploit_scenario: A user on a hostile network is served a plaintext response before HSTS would otherwise force HTTPS, giving an on-path attacker one extra window.
preconditions: Attacker must be on-path for the victim's first connection.
finding.recommendation: Add a Strict-Transport-Security response header (e.g. via middleware) with a sensible max-age.
finding.verifier_reasoning: Confirmed no HSTS header is present in any response inspected.
finding.exploitability_notes: Only affects the narrow first-connection window; TLS is otherwise enforced by the load balancer.

findings.exploitability_notes: Only affects the narrow first-connection window; TLS is otherwise enforced by the load balancer.

finding.title: Dependency with known CVE: requests 2.25.0
finding.description: requirements.txt pins requests==2.25.0, which has a published CVE fixed in a later 2.x release.
finding.impact: Inherits whatever the upstream CVE allows (varies by advisory).
finding.exploit_scenario: Not independently exploitable without a code path that exercises the vulnerable function.
finding.recommendation: Bump the pin to the latest 2.x patch release and re-run the dependency scan.
finding.verifier_reasoning: Version string matched against the advisory database only.
finding.exploitability_notes: Informational — flagged by version match against the advisory database, not by demonstrated exploitation.

findings.exploitability_notes: Informational — flagged by version match against the advisory database, not by demonstrated exploitation.

finding.title: TODO comment references a disabled debug endpoint
finding.verdict_reason: The route is registered behind an `if settings.DEBUG` guard that is False in every deployed environment; not reachable in production.
finding.description: A TODO comment mentions re-enabling a debug endpoint, but the route registration itself is already gated behind a DEBUG flag that is off in all deployed environments.
finding.impact: None in the current deployment configuration.
finding.recommendation: No action required; consider deleting the dead code and comment for clarity.
finding.verifier_reasoning: Verified the guarding conditional evaluates to False in all reviewed environments.
finding.exploitability_notes: Not reachable — confirmed DEBUG=false in every deployment manifest reviewed.

findings.exploitability_notes: Not reachable — confirmed DEBUG=false in every deployment manifest reviewed.

chains.title: Credential leak to account takeover
chains.narrative: The hardcoded AWS credentials (finding 2) grant access to the deployment's S3 artifact bucket, which contains a build image with the JWT signing key. Combined with the alg=none bypass (finding 4), an attacker can forge a session for any account.

chains.title: Injection to credential exposure
chains.narrative: The SQL injection (finding 1) exposes the full payments/users table, including weakly-hashed passwords (finding 9), making offline cracking of those hashes far cheaper than the cost factor was meant to guarantee.
